name: Orange Peel
lede: Orange Peel is a vivid, warm orange-yellow named for the fruit's skin, a color of signs and screens more than of paint.

sections.title: The name
sections.body:
None of the color books we hold treats orange peel as a color. Gurney uses the fruit's skin only as an image: a low sunset ray meets the earth, he says, like a needle entering orange peel at a shallow angle, so the light crosses far more air [1]. Garfield's *Mauve* meets candied orange peel only in a pudding recipe [2].

The color itself is documented by standards. The library's ISCC-NBS block 50 calls it a "vivid orange yellow", and it is close to several RAL paint colors, approximate on screen [3]. The library notes Maerz and Paul's dictionary of 1930 gives 1773 as the first recorded use of the name [3]. It sits near [[orange]], [[amber]] and [[marigold]], with [[tangerine]] a little redder [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 27 carry this color over at least five per cent of the canvas, as photographed [4]. In 41 paintings where we measured its rank, it is an accent in 98 per cent [4]. That fits a color this saturated: a spot of orange against calmer tones [4]. Twenty-three of the matches are from the 1800s, and the earliest dated match is a painting by Filippo Lippi of 1438, a floor not a first [4].

questions.q: How does Gurney use the phrase orange peel?
choices: As an image for sunset light crossing the atmosphere
As a name for a pigment
As a rival to yellow ochre
questions.answer: As an image for sunset light crossing the atmosphere
